title: Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity -- Ch. 8: First Philippine International Bank v. Court of Appeals: Honoring a Perfected Contract
keywords: First Philippine International Bank v. Court of Appeals
Ortigas and Company Limited Partnership vs. Judge Tirso Velasco
Rheem of the Philippines v. Ferrer
rule of law and blind justice
primary_topics: Chapter 8 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' -- CJP's account of First Philippine International Bank v. Court of Appeals, which he singled out as the most significant of the sixteen decisions he wrote in the month after his unanimously carried first ponencia in Ty v. Trampe.

The three holdings of the Decision: that the stockholders' derivative suit filed while the case was pending in the Court of Appeals constituted forum shopping; that a contract of sale of the bank's six parcels of land was perfected at the September 28, 1987 meeting under the doctrine of apparent authority; and that a Central Bank-appointed conservator could not repudiate a validly perfected contract under Section 28-A.

The Epilogue's insistence that sympathy for a distressed bank cannot override respect for perfected contracts, non-impairment of obligations and sanctions against forum shopping, which must be upheld under the rule of law and blind justice, since ruling for the bank because land values had accelerated during long litigation would reward lawlessness and delay.

The Resolution of July 17, 1996 denying the bank's second motion for reconsideration, which restated the doctrine that litigation must end at some point, condemned piecemeal impugnation of judgments, refuted the bank's capital gains tax arithmetic, and rejected its blaming of the Court for a near-bankruptcy caused by its own mismanagement and neglect.
sub_topics: He opened by saying he was uplifted intellectually and morally by his fourteen colleagues' unanimous support for his first ponencia, and resolved to cut his initial caseload of about a thousand cases, writing sixteen more decisions the next month.

He set out the facts: Producers Bank, later First Philippine International Bank, had acquired six parcels of land from BYME; Demetria and Janolo negotiated with Property Management Department manager Mercurio Rivera, offered P3.5 million, were quoted P5.5 million, counter-offered P4.25 million, met senior vice president Luis Co on September 28, 1987, and accepted P5.5 million by letter two days later.

On November 4, 1987 the newly designated acting conservator Leonida T. Encarnacion wrote only that the proposal to buy was being studied by a newly created committee; the bank later rejected the buyers' demands as unauthorized, advertised the properties for sale, and was sued for specific performance.
While the case was pending before the Court of Appeals, Henry Co and other stockholders filed a derivative suit in the RTC to have any perfected sale declared unenforceable.

On the first issue the Court held there was forum shopping, which obtains whenever a party seeks a favorable opinion in another forum after an adverse one, and found identity of parties or interests, of rights asserted and of relief prayed for, such that judgment in one would be res judicata in the other.

On the second issue it found the object and the parties' intent beyond cavil, relied on Deputy Conservator Jose Entereso's testimony that the bank was looking for buyers, and held that Rivera had apparent or implied authority to act for the bank in selling acquired assets.
It treated the perfection of the sale at the September 28, 1987 meeting, as found by the trial court and affirmed by the Court of Appeals, as consistent with human experience, truth and good faith.

On the third issue it held that a conservator's vast powers relate to preserving assets, reorganizing management and restoring viability, and cannot extend to post-facto repudiation of perfected transactions without infringing the non-impairment clause.

It reasoned that if the legislature itself cannot revoke a valid contract it cannot delegate such non-existent power, so the conservator, standing in the place of the board, may only bring court actions to assail defective contracts.
It warned that a contrary reading would let a failing bank become solvent at third parties' expense by unilaterally revoking dealings that had come to look unfavorable.

In the Epilogue the Court acknowledged the bank's overdraft with the Central Bank of P1.023 billion and its plea for rehabilitation, but refused to close its eyes to perfected contracts, non-impairment and the sanctions against forum shopping.

It noted that P5.5 million was reasonable in 1987 for properties the bank had acquired at foreclosure for no more than P3.5 million, and that rewarding the bank for its own procrastination as values rose would reward lawlessness and delay.

The bank filed two motions for reconsideration, the second blaming the Court for its financial malaise; the Resolution of July 17, 1996 denied it outright under the rule barring second motions after a denial with finality.

Quoting Ortigas v. Velasco and In Re Joaquin T. Borromeo, the Resolution held that new grounds or newly discovered errors do not justify a second motion, that piecemeal impugnation of judgments is anathema, and that at some definite time the issues must be laid to rest.

It nonetheless took a last look at the four points raised, reaffirming the forum shopping analysis, pointing to Janolo's September 30, 1987 acceptance letter that the bank never refuted until it was too late, and invoking the rule that findings of fact of the Court of Appeals affirming the trial court deserve great respect and even finality.

It adopted the private respondent's arithmetic that corporations pay 35 percent corporate income tax, not 5 percent capital gains tax, so the tax due was P513,357.60 rather than the P12.625 million the bank claimed, a computation the bank never challenged.

It closed by calling the bank's finger pointing completely misplaced, attributing its almost bankrupt condition to its own mismanagement and neglect, and refusing extra-legal solutions that would override the Court's superior constitutional duty to dispense justice for all.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 8 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' recounted First Philippine International Bank v. Court of Appeals, which CJP called the most significant of the sixteen decisions he wrote in the month after his unanimously supported first ponencia. Buyers Demetrio Demetria and Jose O. Janolo had negotiated for six parcels of land with Mercurio Rivera, the bank's Property Management Department manager, met senior vice president Luis Co on September 28, 1987, and accepted the bank's P5.5 million price by letter two days later; the bank, then under Central Bank conservatorship, later disowned Rivera's dealings, advertised the land for sale, and was sued for specific performance, while its stockholders filed a derivative suit in another court during the appeal. The Court held first that the derivative suit was forum shopping, since the parties, rights and relief were identical enough that judgment in one action would be res judicata in the other; second, that a contract of sale had been perfected at the September 28 meeting, because Rivera had apparent or implied authority and the lower courts' concurrent finding was consistent with human experience, truth and good faith; and third, that a conservator's powers, however vast, relate to preserving assets and restoring viability and cannot extend to post-facto repudiation of perfected transactions without infringing the non-impairment clause. Its Epilogue conceded sympathy for the distressed bank, whose overdraft had reached P1.023 billion, but refused to let that override perfected contracts and the sanctions against forum shopping, noting that rewarding the bank for procrastinating while land values rose would reward lawlessness and delay. When the bank filed a second motion for reconsideration blaming the Court for its malaise, the Resolution of July 17, 1996 denied it outright, restating that litigation must end at some point and that piecemeal impugnation of judgments is anathema, correcting the bank's tax arithmetic from P12.625 million to P513,357.60, and attributing its near-bankruptcy to its own mismanagement and neglect.
